title: Breaking News: Kyoga TV Experiences Theft of Critical Equipment
description:
On July 29, 2025, Kyoga TV suffered a significant setback when their computer, serving as both a playout system and video switcher, was stolen from Omoro Town Council. The incident was promptly reported to Omoro Central Police Station the following morning, and a case was duly recorded.

After a month-long investigation, the suspect was apprehended on August 28, 2025. Kyoga TV's CEO, Mr. Felix Olica, confirmed the development and assured our news team that the station would resume normal operations after clearing with the police.

Mr. Olica strongly condemned the theft, emphasizing its impact on the station's operations. Kyoga TV content remains accessible online through their website (www.kyogatv.com), YouTube, Facebook, TikTok, and X (formerly Twitter).

We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates as more information becomes available.

title: Museveni Urges Lango to Form Committee to Resolve Stalled Cattle Compensation
author: Olica Felix
description:
Museveni Urges Lango to Form Committee to Resolve Stalled Cattle Compensation

Lira, Uganda — President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni has called on the people of Lango sub-region to select a trusted committee to directly engage the government on the long-stalled cattle compensation program, a scheme aimed at compensating families whose livestock and property were destroyed during past insurgencies.

The appeal was made during a meeting at Lango College Grounds on August 17, 2025, where Museveni acknowledged the frustrations of Lango residents over delays, mismanagement, and alleged corruption that have hampered the program since its launch.

The cattle compensation scheme was introduced in 2022 with an allocation of UGX 200 billion, covering victims in Acholi, Lango, and Teso sub-regions. Its objective was to reimburse families for livestock losses during years of conflict and insurgency in northern Uganda. Despite the significant allocation, only UGX 169 billion has been disbursed nationwide, leaving a massive funding gap that has fueled local grievances. Official figures indicate that verified claims alone require UGX 506 billion, while unverified claims total UGX 275 billion, bringing the total estimated need to nearly UGX 800 billion.

Residents of Lango say only UGX 2.5 billion has been successfully disbursed to beneficiaries in the sub-region since 2014. The process has been plagued by several challenges: mismanagement and corruption — with intermediaries, lawyers, and other middlemen allegedly siphoning off funds; fraudulent or inflated claims; payment failures due to invalid or duplicate account details; and the death of rightful beneficiaries, leaving descendants waiting.

Local leaders and residents have demanded reforms to restore trust in the program, including shifting oversight to the Office of the Prime Minister, adopting a household-based payment model, and eliminating middlemen from the process.

Addressing these concerns, President Museveni emphasized the need for a trusted Lango committee to negotiate directly with Kampala. He suggested that verified claims be prioritized, payments be made in a maximum of three instalments to ensure transparency, and that the program be concluded with “certainty and finality.” Museveni highlighted the importance of having representatives who can faithfully communicate the needs and grievances of the Lango people, noting that proper coordination could finally streamline the program.

The prolonged delays and financial mismanagement have heightened frustrations across northern Uganda. Residents view the formation of a committee as a potential solution, but stress that its effectiveness will depend on transparency, proper oversight, and direct engagement with government authorities. The cattle compensation saga has had a lasting impact on the region, affecting livelihoods, agricultural productivity, and family incomes. Many families continue to live with the consequences of the conflict, and unresolved compensation claims exacerbate socio-economic vulnerabilities in Lango.

Officials say forming a select committee, prioritizing verified claims, and ensuring transparent payments could restore faith in the program and address long-standing grievances. Community leaders urge that immediate action be taken to avoid further delays and prevent disputes over unpaid or mismanaged compensation. As pressure mounts on the government to resolve the decades-old compensation issue, the eyes of Lango and the wider northern Uganda region remain on the proposed committee and the President’s directives, with hopes that families finally receive the restitution they have waited for years to obtain.
